context: Maximally structured causal metadata: labels, levels, role, subsystem, clinical description, physiological mechanism, direct parents, direct children, Markov blanket members, CPT shape hints (which parent state combinations dominate each child state), and quantitative clinical notes where available. Designed to provide the richest possible prior for causal graph recovery in the ALARM network.

variables.name: CVP
variables.label: Central venous pressure
variables.description: Right atrial pressure; reflects venous volume status and right-heart preload.
variables.mechanism: CVP is a passive downstream indicator of left ventricular filling volume (LVV) and the backward-pressure effects of left ventricular failure (LVF). It is a terminal leaf: observed for clinical alarms but does not drive any other node.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when LVF=TRUE (backward congestion) or LVV=HIGH; LOW when HYP=TRUE drives LVV=LOW.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal CVP: 2–8 mmHg. CVP < 2 mmHg → LOW (hypovolemia); CVP > 12 mmHg → HIGH (fluid overload or RHF). CVP and PCWP are often dissociated in unilateral ventricular failure.

variables.name: PCWP
variables.label: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
variables.description: Left atrial pressure surrogate; left-heart preload and congestion indicator.
variables.mechanism: PCWP reflects LV filling volume (LVV) and is elevated specifically by LVF through backward pressure transmission into the pulmonary venous circuit. Unlike CVP, PCWP is the most sensitive indicator of left-sided heart failure; normal CVP with elevated PCWP is classic for isolated LVF.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH almost exclusively when LVF=TRUE (pulmonary venous hypertension); LOW when LVV=LOW (hypovolemia). PCWP is more sensitive to LVF than CVP.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal PCWP: 6–12 mmHg. PCWP > 18 mmHg → pulmonary oedema threshold. PCWP < 6 mmHg → hypovolemia. The PCWP–CVP gradient distinguishes LVF (high PCWP, normal/low CVP early) from biventricular failure.

variables.name: HIST
variables.label: Patient history flag
variables.description: Binary prior history flag; encodes baseline cardiac risk.
variables.mechanism: Root node with no modeled parents. A positive history (prior MI, cardiomyopathy) substantially raises the prior probability of LVF. Acts as a purely informational prior modifier; its causal influence in the network flows exclusively through LVF.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIST=TRUE raises P(LVF=TRUE) from baseline ~5% to ~30%.
variables.quantitative_notes: In the ALARM network, HIST is one of three root nodes that directly set LVF probability. Known prior cardiac disease increases perioperative LVF risk approximately 6-fold.

variables.name: TPR
variables.label: Total peripheral resistance
variables.description: Systemic vascular resistance; afterload determinant.
variables.mechanism: TPR is elevated by catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction (CCHL→alpha-adrenergic) and reduced by anaphylaxis-mediated histamine vasodilation (APL). TPR jointly determines blood pressure (BP = CO × TPR) and modulates stroke volume through afterload (high TPR impedes ventricular ejection, reducing STKV).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when CCHL=HIGH and APL=FALSE; LOW when APL=TRUE regardless of CCHL.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal SVR: 800–1200 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. Anaphylaxis can reduce SVR to < 400; catecholamine excess can raise it > 2000. The BP response to TPR change is modulated by CO: low CO with high TPR may still produce LOW BP.

variables.name: BP
variables.label: Blood pressure
variables.description: Systemic arterial pressure; the principal haemodynamic alarm trigger.
variables.mechanism: BP = CO × TPR. It receives influences from both the output pathway (CO, which depends on HR and STKV) and the vascular resistance pathway (TPR, which depends on CCHL and APL). BP feeds the HRBP derived monitoring index. Given CO and TPR, BP is conditionally independent of all other nodes.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: LOW when CO=LOW and TPR=LOW (anaphylaxis + low output — worst case); HIGH when CO=HIGH and TPR=HIGH (catecholamine storm). LOW CO with HIGH TPR may still yield NORMAL BP (compensated state).
variables.quantitative_notes: MAP < 60 mmHg → LOW (organ perfusion threshold); MAP 60–100 → NORMAL; MAP > 100 → HIGH. In ALARM, the LOW state triggers alarm cascades upstream via HRBP and ERLO.

variables.name: CO
variables.label: Cardiac output
variables.description: Heart rate × stroke volume; central perfusion index.
variables.mechanism: CO is the product of HR (rate) and STKV (volume per beat). It determines BP (via TPR) and triggers the ERLO alarm when low. CO is the central haemodynamic node linking the rate pathway (CCHL→HR) and the volume/contractility pathway (HYP/LVF→LVV/STKV).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: LOW when HR=LOW or STKV=LOW; HIGH requires both HR=HIGH and STKV=HIGH. Mixed states (HIGH HR + LOW STKV) typically yield NORMAL or LOW CO.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal CO: 4–8 L/min. CO < 2.5 L/min → cardiogenic shock (LOW); CO > 8 L/min → high-output state (HIGH, e.g., sepsis, catecholamine excess). In ALARM, CO=LOW activates ERLO, which feeds back to CCHL, creating the reflex tachycardia response pattern.

variables.name: HRBP
variables.label: Heart rate / blood pressure index
variables.description: Monitoring index; detects HR/BP dissociation patterns.
variables.mechanism: HRBP is a derived monitoring index computed from the true HR and observed BP. Abnormal states (e.g., HIGH HR with LOW BP = compensated shock; LOW HR with HIGH BP = hypertensive bradycardia) trigger specific alarm patterns. Terminal leaf — no downstream effects.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when HR=HIGH and BP=HIGH; LOW when HR=LOW and BP=LOW. The cross-pattern HR=HIGH/BP=LOW signals compensated low-output state.
variables.quantitative_notes: HRBP is a discretized representation of the shock index (HR/SBP). Shock index > 1 corresponds to HIGH HRBP and indicates haemodynamic compromise.

variables.name: HREK
variables.label: Heart rate from EKG
variables.description: EKG-measured HR; noisy observation of true HR.
variables.mechanism: HREK observes the true HR but is subject to electrocautery artefact (ERCA). When ERCA=TRUE, the EKG signal is corrupted and HREK may not accurately reflect HR. This makes HREK a noisy measurement node — a classic measurement-error structure in Bayesian networks. Terminal leaf.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HREK ≈ HR when ERCA=FALSE; when ERCA=TRUE, HREK is near-uniformly distributed across levels (artefact dominates).
variables.quantitative_notes: Electrocautery frequencies (200–500 kHz) overwhelm standard ECG amplifiers. In ALARM, ERCA=TRUE effectively randomizes HREK, making it unreliable as a HR estimate. This is the primary source of monitoring false alarms in the electrosurgical suite.

variables.name: HRSA
variables.label: Heart rate / oxygen saturation index
variables.description: Monitoring index combining HR and SpO2; detects hypoxic tachycardia.
variables.mechanism: HRSA combines HR and SAO2 to detect the pattern of hypoxic tachycardia (HIGH HR in the setting of LOW SAO2). Terminal leaf — no downstream effects in the model.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: Clinically critical pattern: HIGH HRSA when HR=HIGH and SAO2=LOW (compensatory tachycardia from hypoxia); LOW HRSA when HR=LOW and SAO2=LOW (pre-arrest hypoxic bradycardia).
variables.quantitative_notes: SpO2 < 90% combined with HR > 100 bpm is the canonical hypoxic tachycardia alarm threshold. In ALARM this maps to SAO2=LOW + HR=HIGH → HRSA=HIGH.

variables.name: PAP
variables.label: Pulmonary artery pressure
variables.description: Pulmonary arterial pressure; elevated by PE or LVF.
variables.mechanism: PAP is raised by two independent mechanisms: PMB (obstructs pulmonary vasculature, acutely raises right ventricular afterload) and LVF (backward congestion raises pulmonary venous and arterial pressures). These two causes produce distinct clinical patterns: PMB raises PAP with normal/low PCWP; LVF raises both PAP and PCWP. Terminal leaf.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when either PMB=TRUE or LVF=TRUE; LOW extremely rare (only in severe right-heart dysfunction). The PAP/PCWP combination distinguishes PE (HIGH PAP + LOW/NORMAL PCWP) from LVF (HIGH PAP + HIGH PCWP).
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal mean PAP: 10–20 mmHg. Mean PAP > 25 mmHg → pulmonary hypertension. Acute PE can raise mean PAP to 30–40 mmHg. In ALARM, HIGH PAP with HIGH PCWP strongly implicates LVF; HIGH PAP with NORMAL PCWP implicates PMB.

variables.name: SAO2
variables.label: Arterial oxygen saturation
variables.description: Arterial O2 saturation; key hypoxaemia alarm indicator.
variables.mechanism: SAO2 is determined by pulmonary venous saturation (PVS, set by FIO2 and VALV) and intrapulmonary shunt (SHNT). High SHNT reduces SAO2 even with adequate ventilation and FIO2 (shunt-refractory hypoxaemia). SAO2 feeds HRSA monitoring index.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: LOW when SHNT=HIGH regardless of PVS (shunt-refractory); LOW when PVS=LOW and SHNT=NORMAL; HIGH only possible when PVS=HIGH and SHNT=NORMAL.
variables.quantitative_notes: SpO2 < 90% (PaO2 < 60 mmHg) → LOW; 90–95% → borderline; > 95% → NORMAL; > 99% → HIGH. The shunt fraction required to produce SpO2 < 90% is approximately 30% of cardiac output.

variables.name: FIO2
variables.label: Fraction of inspired oxygen
variables.description: Ventilator O2 setting; root determinant of oxygen delivery.
variables.mechanism: Root node set by the clinician. FIO2 is the primary oxygen-delivery input, setting alveolar PO2 via the alveolar gas equation. It directly determines pulmonary venous saturation (PVS). FIO2=LOW represents a delivery error (e.g., empty O2 source, wrong gas). Its influence on SAO2 is fully mediated through PVS.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: FIO2=LOW: P(PVS=LOW) increases substantially even with normal VALV; FIO2=NORMAL: PVS is determined primarily by VALV.
variables.quantitative_notes: Room air FIO2 = 0.21 → LOW in ALARM context (implies suboptimal O2 delivery in a monitored patient). FIO2 = 0.40–1.0 → NORMAL for intubated ICU/OR patient. Increasing FIO2 corrects non-shunt hypoxaemia but cannot correct shunt-refractory hypoxaemia.

variables.name: PRSS
variables.label: Breathing circuit pressure
variables.description: Observed circuit pressure; reflects tube-level ventilation.
variables.mechanism: PRSS is driven by VTUB: the gas pressure at the tube/circuit interface rises proportionally with delivered gas volume. ZERO pressure is pathognomonic of complete disconnection (DISC=TRUE) or VMCH=ZERO. HIGH pressure indicates obstruction distal to the measurement point (e.g., KINK). Terminal leaf.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ZERO when VTUB=ZERO (disconnection or machine failure); HIGH when VTUB=HIGH but VLNG=LOW (obstruction pattern: gas delivered but not reaching lungs); NORMAL when all upstream states are NORMAL.
variables.quantitative_notes: Peak inspiratory pressure > 40 cmH2O → HIGH (barotrauma risk / obstruction); PIP = 0 → ZERO (disconnection). The PRSS–MINV dissociation is diagnostically important: high PRSS with low MINV implies tube obstruction; zero PRSS with zero MINV implies circuit disconnection.

variables.name: ECO2
variables.label: Expired CO2
variables.description: End-tidal CO2; alveolar ventilation and metabolism indicator.
variables.mechanism: ECO2 is the downstream gas-exchange product of alveolar ventilation (VALV). ZERO ECO2 is pathognomonic of esophageal intubation (INT=ESOPHAGEAL) or complete circuit disconnection — no gas exchange occurring. ECO2 is the most rapid indicator of catastrophic ventilation failure. Terminal leaf.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ZERO when VALV=ZERO (esophageal intubation, disconnection); LOW when VALV=LOW (partial obstruction, one-lung ventilation); HIGH when VALV=HIGH and metabolic rate is elevated.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal EtCO2: 35–45 mmHg → NORMAL. EtCO2 = 0 → ZERO (no pulmonary circulation/ventilation). EtCO2 < 20 mmHg → LOW (massive PE, CPR, low VALV). EtCO2 > 50 mmHg → HIGH (hypoventilation, metabolic acidosis compensation). The EtCO2 waveform's return after intubation confirms tracheal placement.

variables.name: MINV
variables.label: Minute ventilation (observed)
variables.description: Measured minute ventilation; can deviate from machine output.
variables.mechanism: MINV is observed at the lung level and reflects VLNG. The key diagnostic use of MINV in ALARM is its dissociation from VMCH: VMCH=NORMAL + MINV=ZERO indicates a fault between machine and lungs (DISC, KINK, or INT=ESOPHAGEAL). Terminal measurement leaf.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: MINV ≈ VLNG when measurement is accurate; ZERO when VLNG=ZERO (any complete ventilation fault); discrepancy between VMCH and MINV is the primary fault-detection signal.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal minute ventilation: 6–10 L/min. MINV < 2 L/min → LOW (hypoventilation alarm threshold). MINV = 0 → ZERO (circuit fault). MINV > 15 L/min → HIGH (hyperventilation). The MINV–VMCH gap quantifies circuit loss.

variables.name: MVS
variables.label: Minute ventilation set (target)
variables.description: Clinician-set ventilation target; root of the ventilation delivery chain.
variables.mechanism: Root node. MVS is set by the clinician based on patient size and ventilatory requirements. It is the upstream input to VMCH and therefore the starting point of the entire ventilation delivery cascade. No parents in the model.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: MVS=NORMAL → VMCH=NORMAL (assuming machine function). MVS=LOW → deliberate hypoventilation (permissive hypercapnia strategy).
variables.quantitative_notes: MVS is set per ideal body weight: typically 6–8 mL/kg tidal volume × 12–16 bpm = 5–8 L/min for NORMAL. In ALARM, MVS serves as the sole ventilatory prescription input — it is the only root node in the ventilation subsystem that a clinician directly controls.

variables.name: HYP
variables.label: Hypovolemia
variables.description: Reduced circulating blood volume; primary preload cause.
variables.mechanism: Root node. HYP reduces left ventricular preload (LVV→LOW), which by Frank-Starling reduces stroke volume (STKV→LOW), then CO, and ultimately BP. The haemodynamic fingerprint of hypovolemia is LOW CVP + LOW PCWP + LOW CO + LOW BP with preserved TPR and high CCHL (reflex).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HYP=TRUE → P(LVV=LOW) ≈ 0.85; P(LVV=NORMAL) ≈ 0.14; P(LVV=HIGH) ≈ 0.01.
variables.quantitative_notes: Defined as circulating blood volume deficit > 15% (Class II shock). Haemoglobin may initially be normal (no haemodilution yet). Key distinction from LVF: hypovolemia has LOW PCWP, while LVF has HIGH PCWP. In ALARM, HYP and LVF produce similar low-output patterns but different filling-pressure patterns.

variables.name: LVF
variables.label: Left ventricular failure
variables.description: Impaired LV contractility; raises filling pressures and reduces output.
variables.mechanism: Partially a root node (modulated by HIST). LVF reduces stroke volume by impairing contractility (reduced ejection fraction), simultaneously raising left-sided filling pressures (PCWP, CVP) and pulmonary artery pressure (PAP). It is causally upstream of five nodes and is the most connected root cause in the cardiovascular subnetwork.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: LVF=TRUE → P(STKV=LOW) ≈ 0.75; P(PCWP=HIGH) ≈ 0.80; P(PAP=HIGH) ≈ 0.55. HIST=TRUE raises P(LVF=TRUE) approximately 6-fold.
variables.quantitative_notes: EF < 40% defines systolic LVF. LVF produces the classic haemodynamic triad: low CO, high PCWP (>18 mmHg), high SVR (compensatory). In ALARM, LVF is the single most consequential root cause: it has the most downstream effects and is the primary driver of the ERLO alarm cascade.

variables.name: APL
variables.label: Anaphylaxis
variables.description: Severe systemic allergic reaction; causes acute vasodilation.
variables.mechanism: Root node. APL releases histamine, which directly reduces TPR via arteriolar dilation and increases capillary permeability (reducing circulating volume). This produces the anaphylactic shock pattern: LOW TPR + LOW BP despite initially preserved or HIGH CO (high-output shock). Its effect on TPR is the strongest single-cause TPR reduction in the model.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: APL=TRUE → P(TPR=LOW) ≈ 0.90, P(BP=LOW) elevated even if CO=NORMAL.
variables.quantitative_notes: Anaphylactic shock: median time to cardiovascular collapse < 30 min after antigen exposure. SVR can fall to < 200 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. Distinguishable from cardiogenic shock by LOW TPR (vs HIGH in cardiogenic) and normal/HIGH CO early.

variables.name: ANES
variables.label: Insufficient anesthesia / analgesia
variables.description: Pain/awareness under anaesthesia; triggers sympathetic activation.
variables.mechanism: Root node. Inadequate anaesthetic depth activates the sympatho-adrenal axis, raising circulating catecholamines (CCHL). This is the primary intraoperative cause of catecholamine excess. CCHL then drives HR and TPR upward, producing the hypertensive tachycardia pattern of awareness under anaesthesia.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ANES=TRUE → P(CCHL=HIGH) ≈ 0.70. In the absence of ERLO feedback, ANES is the dominant driver of CCHL=HIGH in the ALARM model.
variables.quantitative_notes: Intraoperative awareness incidence: 0.1–0.2%. The sympathetic response produces HR > 100 bpm and SBP > 160 mmHg in approximately 80% of aware patients. In ALARM, ANES=TRUE is the primary root cause of the tachycardia + hypertension alarm pattern.

variables.name: PMB
variables.label: Pulmonary embolus
variables.description: Pulmonary vascular obstruction; raises PAP and creates V/Q mismatch.
variables.mechanism: Root node. PMB simultaneously (a) obstructs pulmonary vasculature → HIGH PAP (right ventricular strain) and (b) creates V/Q mismatch → HIGH SHNT → LOW SAO2. This dual cardiovascular-oxygenation effect makes PMB the only root cause node that bridges both subsystems.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: PMB=TRUE → P(PAP=HIGH) ≈ 0.85, P(SHNT=HIGH) ≈ 0.80. The joint PAP=HIGH + SAO2=LOW pattern with normal PCWP is pathognomonic for PE vs LVF.
variables.quantitative_notes: Massive PE (> 50% vascular occlusion): PAP rises acutely to 35–40 mmHg; SpO2 drops to 80–88%. Distinguishing features from LVF in ALARM: PE → HIGH PAP + LOW/NORMAL PCWP + HIGH SHNT; LVF → HIGH PAP + HIGH PCWP + NORMAL SHNT.

variables.name: INT
variables.label: Intubation status
variables.description: ETT placement; determines whether ventilation reaches the trachea/lungs.
variables.mechanism: Root node. INT governs whether tube-delivered gas (VTUB) reaches the lungs: ESOPHAGEAL → all gas enters the esophagus, VLNG=ZERO; ONESIDED → gas goes to one bronchus, VLNG reduced by ~50%; NORMAL → full VTUB reaches lungs. INT is the highest-impact single fault in the ventilation pathway.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ESOPHAGEAL → P(VLNG=ZERO)=1; ONESIDED → P(VLNG=LOW)≈0.90; NORMAL → VLNG determined by VTUB.
variables.quantitative_notes: Esophageal intubation incidence in emergency intubations: ~1–5%. ZERO ECO2 + ZERO MINV despite VMCH=NORMAL is the ALARM signature of esophageal intubation. ONESIDED intubation (usually right main-stem) produces unilateral breath sounds and SpO2 drop within 1–2 minutes.

variables.name: KINK
variables.label: Kinked breathing tube
variables.description: ETT kinking; obstructs gas flow and reduces VTUB.
variables.mechanism: Root node. KINK obstructs the lumen of the ETT, reducing VTUB proportionally (partial kink → LOW, complete kink → ZERO). KINK produces the HIGH PRSS (pressure builds up proximal to obstruction) + LOW MINV pattern. It is one of two mechanical root causes of VTUB reduction (the other being DISC).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: KINK=TRUE → P(VTUB=LOW or ZERO) ≈ 0.85. Distinguishable from DISC by PRSS pattern: KINK → HIGH PRSS (obstruction); DISC → ZERO PRSS (open circuit).
variables.quantitative_notes: Kinking most common at the teeth/lips or when the neck is flexed. HIGH PIP (> 40 cmH2O) with LOW MINV is the classic kink alarm pattern. Resolves immediately with straightening the tube.

variables.name: DISC
variables.label: Circuit disconnection
variables.description: Breathing circuit separation; eliminates all gas delivery.
variables.mechanism: Root node. DISC completely breaks the gas-delivery circuit, reducing VTUB to ZERO irrespective of VMCH output. DISC produces ZERO PRSS + ZERO MINV + ZERO ECO2 — the complete ventilation failure pattern. It is the most immediately life-threatening ventilation fault and the highest-priority alarm in ALARM.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: DISC=TRUE → P(VTUB=ZERO) ≈ 0.98. The PRSS=ZERO + MINV=ZERO + ECO2=ZERO triad at VMCH=NORMAL is pathognomonic for DISC.
variables.quantitative_notes: Complete disconnection produces apnoea within one breath. SpO2 begins to fall within 30–90 seconds. The ALARM network encodes disconnection as the highest-urgency fault because all three downstream ventilation alarms (PRSS, MINV, ECO2) simultaneously reach ZERO.

variables.name: LVV
variables.label: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume
variables.description: LV preload; the Frank-Starling determinant of stroke volume.
variables.mechanism: LVV is determined by circulating volume (HYP reduces it) and by LVF (impaired emptying may paradoxically raise residual volume in dilated cardiomyopathy). By the Frank-Starling relationship, LVV directly and monotonically determines STKV across the physiological range. It is also the primary driver of venous filling pressures CVP and PCWP.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: LVV=LOW when HYP=TRUE (overwhelmingly); LVV=HIGH possible when LVF=TRUE (dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle). LVV is the key mediating node between HYP and all filling-pressure/output variables.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal LVEDV: 120–140 mL. LVEDV < 70 mL → hypovolemic (LOW). LVEDV > 200 mL → dilated LVF (HIGH). Frank-Starling optimum is approximately LVEDP 12–15 mmHg; above this, further filling yields diminishing STKV returns.

variables.name: STKV
variables.label: Stroke volume
variables.description: Volume ejected per heartbeat; central output integrator.
variables.mechanism: STKV integrates three physiological determinants: preload (LVV — Frank-Starling), contractility (LVF — reduces ejection fraction), and afterload (TPR — high afterload impedes ejection). It is the direct multiplicative factor in CO = HR × STKV and is the single most important intermediate node connecting root causes to the CO alarm.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: LOW when LVF=TRUE (dominant effect) or LVV=LOW (preload limitation); HIGH requires LVV=HIGH + LVF=FALSE + TPR=LOW. HIGH TPR reduces STKV even with normal preload and contractility.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal SV: 60–100 mL. SV < 40 mL → LOW; SV > 100 mL → HIGH. Ejection fraction = SV/LVEDV; EF < 40% (LVF) reduces SV primarily. The Anrep effect (afterload-SV relationship) means TPR = HIGH can reduce SV by 15–25% even with normal contractility.

variables.name: CCHL
variables.label: Catecholamine level
variables.description: Circulating catecholamines; drives HR and vasoconstriction.
variables.mechanism: CCHL is elevated by two inputs: ANES (sympathetic activation from pain/awareness) and ERLO (baroreceptor-mediated reflex response to low CO). CCHL then drives two downstream effects: HR (beta-1 chronotropy) and TPR (alpha-1 vasoconstriction). This creates the key feedback loop: low CO → ERLO → CCHL → HR → CO (partial correction).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when ANES=TRUE OR ERLO=TRUE. When both are TRUE, P(CCHL=HIGH) is near 1. When both FALSE, P(CCHL=NORMAL) ≈ 0.95.
variables.quantitative_notes: Plasma epinephrine > 500 pg/mL or norepinephrine > 2000 pg/mL → HIGH. In the ALARM model CCHL is binary (NORMAL/HIGH), encoding the clinically relevant threshold between physiological and pathological sympathetic activation. The CCHL→HR→CO→ERLO→CCHL feedback loop is the primary compensatory mechanism for low output.

variables.name: ERLO
variables.label: Error / low output flag
variables.description: Low-output alarm; triggers catecholamine reflex and clinical alert.
variables.mechanism: ERLO is triggered by low CO. It then activates the baroreceptor-mediated catecholamine response (CCHL), forming the only feedback loop in the ALARM network: CO → ERLO → CCHL → HR → CO. This feedback is the physiological compensation for low output but is also the source of reflex tachycardia/hypertension alarms.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ERLO=TRUE when CO=LOW (threshold alarm); P(ERLO=TRUE | CO=LOW) ≈ 0.90.
variables.quantitative_notes: ERLO is one of the key alarm nodes in ALARM. Low CO (< 2.5 L/min) triggers ERLO. The ERLO → CCHL → HR → CO feedback is the model's representation of the Bezold-Jarisch reflex and baroreceptor-mediated compensation. The loop typically partially corrects CO by raising HR, explaining compensated low-output states.

variables.name: HR
variables.label: Heart rate
variables.description: Heart rate; rate component of cardiac output.
variables.mechanism: HR is driven by CCHL (beta-1 adrenergic chronotropy). It is one of the two multiplicative factors in CO = HR × STKV and simultaneously feeds three monitoring indices: HRBP (with BP), HREK (with ERCA noise), and HRSA (with SAO2). HR is the central hub node of the HR monitoring subsystem.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when CCHL=HIGH; LOW when CCHL=NORMAL and intrinsic conduction is impaired. P(HR=HIGH | CCHL=HIGH) ≈ 0.80.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal HR: 60–100 bpm. HR < 50 → LOW; HR > 110 → HIGH. Beta-1 stimulation raises HR by 20–50 bpm acutely. HR is the most frequently alarmed parameter in perioperative monitoring. In ALARM, HR is a 4-parent-child hub: it is both a physiological intermediate (→CO) and a monitoring source (→HRBP, HREK, HRSA).

variables.name: ERCA
variables.label: Electrocautery in use
variables.description: Surgical electrocautery active; corrupts EKG measurement.
variables.mechanism: Root node. ERCA introduces high-frequency (200–500 kHz) electrical interference that overwhelms the ECG amplifier, making HREK an unreliable HR measurement. It does not affect the underlying physiology — only the fidelity of the HREK observation. This is a canonical measurement-error / instrumentation-noise node in the ALARM network.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ERCA=TRUE → HREK is approximately uniformly distributed across LOW/NORMAL/HIGH (random noise). ERCA=FALSE → HREK closely tracks HR.
variables.quantitative_notes: Electrocautery is used in > 90% of surgical procedures. It generates EMI at 0.3–3 MHz. The ALARM network models ERCA as the sole source of HREK unreliability. During ERCA=TRUE, the only reliable HR monitoring is pulse oximetry (HRSA) or arterial line (HRBP) — not the EKG.

variables.name: SHNT
variables.label: Intrapulmonary shunt
variables.description: Fraction of CO bypassing ventilated alveoli; causes O2-refractory hypoxaemia.
variables.mechanism: SHNT is elevated by PMB (V/Q mismatch from vascular obstruction) and by inadequate alveolar ventilation (VALV=LOW or ZERO — atelectasis, one-lung ventilation). HIGH SHNT reduces SAO2 in a manner refractory to FIO2 increase — the defining feature of shunt physiology.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when PMB=TRUE OR VALV=ZERO (complete atelectasis from esophageal/one-sided intubation); NORMAL when VALV=NORMAL and PMB=FALSE.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal shunt fraction (Qs/Qt): < 5%. Qs/Qt > 25–30% → SAO2 < 90% despite FIO2=1.0. In ALARM, SHNT bridges the ventilation subsystem (through VALV) and the cardiovascular subsystem (through PMB), making it the key cross-subsystem oxygenation node.

variables.name: PVS
variables.label: Pulmonary venous oxygen saturation
variables.description: O2 saturation of blood leaving the lungs; set by FIO2 and alveolar ventilation.
variables.mechanism: PVS is determined by alveolar PO2, which depends on both FIO2 (O2 delivery to alveoli) and VALV (ventilation to clear CO2 and maintain alveolar PO2). PVS feeds SAO2, where shunt (SHNT) mixes unventilated blood and reduces the final arterial saturation.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: PVS=HIGH when FIO2=NORMAL and VALV=NORMAL or HIGH; PVS=LOW when FIO2=LOW or VALV=ZERO. The interaction: high FIO2 can partially compensate for low VALV (nitrogen washout effect).
variables.quantitative_notes: Alveolar PO2 = FIO2 × (Patm − PH2O) − PaCO2/RQ ≈ FIO2 × 713 − PaCO2/0.8. PVS=HIGH corresponds to end-capillary PO2 > 100 mmHg (saturation ≈ 100%). LOW FIO2 (room air in intubated patient) → PVS=LOW, with alveolar PO2 ≈ 100 mmHg.

variables.name: ACO2
variables.label: Arterial CO2
variables.description: PaCO2; inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation.
variables.mechanism: ACO2 is determined by alveolar ventilation (VALV): VA = VCO2 / (PaCO2 × K). Hypoventilation (VALV=LOW/ZERO) raises ACO2; hyperventilation (VALV=HIGH) lowers it. ACO2 is the gold-standard ventilatory adequacy measure and a terminal leaf in the oxygenation pathway.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: HIGH when VALV=LOW or ZERO (hypercapnic respiratory failure); LOW when VALV=HIGH (hyperventilation); NORMAL when VALV=NORMAL.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal PaCO2: 35–45 mmHg → NORMAL. PaCO2 < 30 mmHg → LOW (hyperventilation/respiratory alkalosis). PaCO2 > 50 mmHg → HIGH (hypercapnia/respiratory acidosis). PaCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation: doubling VA halves PaCO2. In ALARM, ACO2 and ECO2 are redundant ventilation sufficiency indicators that together confirm VALV state.

variables.name: VALV
variables.label: Alveolar ventilation
variables.description: Effective gas-exchange ventilation; lung ventilation minus dead space.
variables.mechanism: VALV is derived from VLNG (total lung ventilation minus anatomical dead space ~150 mL/breath). VALV is the final common pathway of all ventilation effects: it simultaneously drives CO2 removal (ACO2 inverse relationship), O2 delivery (PVS via alveolar PO2), expired CO2 signal (ECO2), and shunt magnitude (SHNT via atelectasis). It is the highest-fanout intermediate node in the ventilation subnetwork.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ZERO when VLNG=ZERO (esophageal intubation, disconnection); LOW when VLNG=LOW (one-lung, kink); NORMAL when VLNG=NORMAL. The VALV node is the key information bottleneck: all four downstream oxygenation/ventilation measurements become conditionally independent of upstream faults given VALV.
variables.quantitative_notes: Normal alveolar ventilation: 4–5 L/min (minute ventilation 6–8 L/min minus dead space ~150 mL × 12–16 bpm = 1.8–2.4 L/min). VALV=ZERO (no alveolar exchange) → all four children reach alarm-level abnormality within 2–3 minutes. VALV is the single most consequential intermediate node for patient safety in the ALARM network.

variables.name: VLNG
variables.label: Lung ventilation
variables.description: Total ventilation reaching the lungs; penultimate ventilation delivery node.
variables.mechanism: VLNG is determined by VTUB (gas arriving at the trachea) modified by INT (intubation status). ESOPHAGEAL INT forces VLNG=ZERO; ONESIDED reduces it to ~50%. Normal INT means VLNG ≈ VTUB. VLNG then feeds VALV (alveolar exchange) and MINV (observed ventilation measurement).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ZERO when INT=ESOPHAGEAL or VTUB=ZERO; LOW when INT=ONESIDED or VTUB=LOW; NORMAL when INT=NORMAL and VTUB=NORMAL.
variables.quantitative_notes: VLNG is the interface between the 'delivery' sub-chain (MVS→VMCH→VTUB) and the 'exchange' sub-chain (VALV and its children). The MINV sensor monitors VLNG: the VLNG–VMCH discrepancy is the primary diagnostic signal for circuit faults. VLNG=NORMAL with VALV=ZERO would indicate pure dead-space ventilation (not modeled separately in ALARM).

variables.name: VTUB
variables.label: Tube ventilation
variables.description: Gas flow at the ETT; subject to mechanical circuit faults.
variables.mechanism: VTUB is the machine output (VMCH) after passing through two series fault gates: KINK (tube obstruction, reduces/blocks gas) and DISC (circuit break, zeroes gas delivery). These faults combine multiplicatively: either alone can reduce VTUB to ZERO. VTUB then determines VLNG (via INT) and PRSS (circuit pressure).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ZERO when DISC=TRUE (dominates) or KINK=TRUE (partial/complete); LOW when VMCH=LOW or partial KINK; NORMAL when VMCH=NORMAL + KINK=FALSE + DISC=FALSE.
variables.quantitative_notes: VTUB is the key fault-integration node: it receives inputs from three root faults (VMCH level, KINK, DISC). The PRSS–VLNG combination at VTUB's children discriminates fault type: VTUB→HIGH PRSS + LOW VLNG = obstruction distal to pressure sensor; VTUB=ZERO + PRSS=ZERO = disconnection. In ALARM, VTUB is the most diagnostically central node in the ventilation delivery sub-chain.

variables.name: VMCH
variables.label: Ventilator machine output
variables.description: Mechanical ventilator gas delivery; set by MVS.
variables.mechanism: VMCH is driven by the clinician-set minute ventilation (MVS). It is the first node in the ventilation delivery cascade. The diagnostic significance of VMCH lies in its dissociation from downstream measurements: VMCH=NORMAL with MINV=ZERO or PRSS=ZERO indicates a fault downstream (DISC, KINK, or INT). VMCH=ZERO with all others ZERO indicates a machine or MVS fault.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: VMCH closely tracks MVS: NORMAL when MVS=NORMAL; LOW when MVS=LOW. Machine failure (VMCH=ZERO at MVS=NORMAL) is rare but modeled.
variables.quantitative_notes: Modern ICU ventilators deliver MVS with < 5% error under normal conditions. VMCH=ZERO at non-zero MVS indicates ventilator malfunction (rare: < 0.01% per hour). The VMCH node in ALARM serves primarily as the interface between clinician intent (MVS) and the mechanical delivery system (VTUB), enabling fault localization by comparing MVS, VMCH, and MINV simultaneously.
